Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Work & responsibility · Civic life: news, government & the law

unemployment noun and adjective

also unemployed, out of work, jobless, be out of work, lose one’s job, on the dole

our formation

quaestū carēre

to be out of work

A plain description: to lack a living (quaestus, see employment), as Plautus describes the poor, quibus nec quaestus est (Rud. 2.1.2). The unemployed are quī quaestū carent.

Other words

  • operā carēns — unemployed

    also used · modern · M-O s.v. unemployed

  • invīta operis vacātiō — unemployment (the condition)

    also used · modern · M-O s.v. unemployment, after Egger

    Egger’s phrase: freedom from work that is not wanted. Ōtiōsus, which Lewis & Short glosses “unemployed”, means at leisure or without public office, a condition a Roman chose, so it does not say out of work.

Examples

  • pauperēs hominēs, quibus nec quaestus est

    poor men, who have no livingPlaut. Rud. 2.1.2 (Lewis & Short)

  • Frāter ejus jam sex mēnsēs quaestū caret.

    His brother has been out of work for six months now.composed

See also employment, fire, job.

SourcesLewis & Short: quaestus · Lewis & Short: careo · Lewis & Short: vacatio · Lewis & Short: otiosus

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. unemployed, unemployment.

The example sentence marked “composed” is ours.
